lessons.title: NBA structure and the 82-game season
lessons.objective: Describe conferences, divisions and the shape of a season.

payload.prompt: How many teams are in the NBA?

options.text: 30 teams divided into two conferences of 15 teams each.
24 teams in one league.
32 teams split evenly by division.

explanation.correct: The league has 30 teams, split into an Eastern and a Western Conference of 15 each. The two conferences only meet in the NBA Finals.
explanation.incorrect: The NBA has 30 teams, not 24 or 32. They sit in two conferences, East and West, with 15 teams in each.

payload.prompt: Are conferences and divisions the same thing?

scene.alt: A diagram of the NBA: two conferences, each split into three divisions of five teams.

explanation.correct: A conference contains three divisions of five teams each. Divisions matter for scheduling, since teams play division rivals four times a year, but seeding follows the whole conference.
explanation.incorrect: Divisions are sub-groups inside a conference: three divisions of five teams in each. Conferences are the bigger groups, and seeding follows the conference standings.

payload.prompt: How many regular-season games does each NBA team play?

options.text: 82 games, including every other team at least twice.
72 games and then the playoffs start.
100 games in a calendar year.

explanation.correct: An NBA team plays 82 games from October through April: four against each division rival, three or four against the rest of its conference, and two against every team in the other conference.
explanation.incorrect: The regular season is 82 games, not 72 or 100. Half are at home and half are on the road, and every team appears on the schedule at least twice.

payload.prompt: Fill in the NBA's conference structure.
payload.template: The NBA has two {{conf}}, the East and the West, with {{teams}} teams in each. Inside each one are three {{div}}.

explanation.correct: The league is split into the East and West conferences with 15 teams each. Atlantic, Central and Pacific are divisions inside those conferences.
explanation.incorrect: The two big groups are the East and the West, with 15 teams in each. Atlantic, Central, Pacific and Southwest are divisions, which sit inside the conferences.

payload.prompt: Roughly how many months does the NBA regular season last?

explanation.correct: The regular season runs about six months, from late October to mid-April. The Play-In and then the playoffs follow, and the Finals end in June.
explanation.incorrect: The NBA regular season lasts about six months, from late October to mid-April. It feels long because 82 games fit in a little over a hundred and fifty days.

lessons.title: Standings, seeds and tiebreakers
lessons.objective: Explain seeding and why the 7th seed matters.

payload.prompt: What determines playoff seeding?

options.text: Win-loss record inside each conference, with tiebreakers for ties.
How many All-Stars a team has.
Whether a team won its division.

explanation.correct: Each conference is ranked by record: the best record is the 1-seed, the next best the 2-seed, and so on. Winning a division used to guarantee a top-four seed, but today record alone decides.
explanation.incorrect: Seeds follow the standings inside each conference, not All-Star counts or division titles. A team with a division title and a worse record than a rival is seeded below that rival.

payload.prompt: Match each seeding term to what it means.

pairs.definition: The best record in the conference. It plays the lowest-seeded qualifier in round one.
In a best-of-seven, the higher seed hosts games 1, 2, 5 and 7.
A set of rules, starting with head-to-head record, that separates teams with the same record.

distractorDefinitions: A team that did not make the playoffs.
The worst record in the league.

explanation.summary: Record sets the seed, the tiebreaker splits ties, and a better seed earns home-court advantage, which means more games in its own arena.

payload.prompt: Order how a conference's final seeds are set.

items.text: Teams are ranked by win-loss record after game 82.
Tiebreakers separate teams with identical records.
items.why: Ties are common, and head-to-head record is checked first.

items.text: Seeds 1 to 6 go straight to the playoffs.
items.why: The top six avoid the Play-In.

items.text: Seeds 7 to 10 enter the Play-In for the last two spots.
items.why: The Play-In settles what the standings leave open.

explanation.correct: Record ranks the teams, tiebreakers settle ties, and then the standings split into two groups: the top six go straight in, and seeds 7 to 10 play for the last two spots.
explanation.incorrect: The order is rank by record, break ties, lock in the top six, and send seeds 7 to 10 to the Play-In. Tiebreakers have to come before the top six are fixed.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: If we win out, we might jump from 6 to 2 in the standings.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: If her team keeps winning, it could climb from the 6th seed to the 2nd.
Her team is switching to a different division.
Her team gets to choose its own seed.
The league assigns seeds by television ratings.

payload.translation: 'Win out' means winning every game left. She is saying a winning streak would push her team's record past several others and move it up the standings.

followUps.line: It also depends on the teams above you, right?
followUps.why: Seeding is relative, so what other teams do matters, and it shows you get that.
It is an easy question that gauges how realistic the climb is.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Seeds just follow the standings. 'Win out' means winning every remaining game, and a seed can jump quickly near the end.

lessons.title: The Play-In Tournament
lessons.objective: Walk through the 7-10 seed play-in bracket.

payload.prompt: Order the Play-In, from the opening games to the last spot.

items.text: The 7 vs 8 winner takes the 7th playoff seed.
items.why: A winner of the top game is safe.

items.text: The 7 vs 8 loser hosts the 9 vs 10 winner for the 8th seed.
items.why: It is the last game, and the loser is out.

explanation.correct: The opening games sort the four teams: the 7 vs 8 winner is in as the 7-seed, the 9 vs 10 loser is out, and the last game decides the 8-seed. The top two seeds get a second chance.
explanation.incorrect: The order is the opening games, the 7 vs 8 winner locking in the 7 spot, and then the loser of that game meeting the winner of 9 vs 10 for the 8 spot.

payload.prompt: The 9-seed beats the 10-seed in the Play-In. Is it in the playoffs?

scene.alt: A Play-In bracket: the 9-seed has just beaten the 10-seed, and the loser of the 7 vs 8 game is waiting for the winner.

explanation.correct: The 9 vs 10 winner only earns one more game: it has to beat the loser of the 7 vs 8 game to take the 8th seed. The 10-seed is out for good.
explanation.incorrect: The Play-In is two chances for seeds 7 and 8 and only one for seeds 9 and 10. Beating the 10-seed just keeps the 9-seed alive for a game against the loser of 7 vs 8.

payload.prompt: What is the Play-In Tournament?

options.text: An extra tournament between seeds 7-10 to determine the final two playoff spots.
A tournament to decide the NBA champion.
A warmup for All-Star weekend.

explanation.correct: The Play-In is for the teams that just missed the top six. Seeds 7 to 10 in each conference play a short bracket to decide the 7th and 8th playoff seeds.
explanation.incorrect: It is not the title tournament or an All-Star event. The Play-In is a short bracket for seeds 7 to 10 that fills the last two playoff spots in each conference.

payload.prompt: Why do teams want to be the 6-seed or better?

options.text: A top-six seed skips the Play-In and cannot miss the playoffs.
A top-six seed is awarded a trophy.
Seventh seeds are not allowed to win a series.

explanation.correct: The top six seeds go straight to round one. Seeds 7 to 10 risk being eliminated in the Play-In, so a few extra wins in the regular season matter a lot.
explanation.incorrect: There is no trophy for a top-six finish and no rule against a 7-seed winning a series. The real prize is skipping the Play-In and locking up a playoff spot.

payload.prompt: The 8-seed beats the 7-seed in the Play-In. New seed?

scene.alt: A Play-In bracket: the 8-seed has just beaten the 7-seed in the opening game.

explanation.correct: The winner of the 7 vs 8 game takes the 7th playoff seed, whichever team it was. The loser still has a second chance for the 8th seed.
explanation.incorrect: Play-In seeds are not fixed. The winner of the opening 7 vs 8 game becomes the 7-seed, so an 8-seed that wins jumps up to 7.

lessons.title: The playoffs
lessons.objective: Explain the four best-of-seven rounds and playoff vocabulary.

payload.prompt: Order the playoff rounds from start to finish.

items.text: Round 1: Four matchups per conference (1 vs 8, 2 vs 7, 3 vs 6, 4 vs 5).
items.why: First round is seeded by record from the regular season.

items.text: Conference Semifinals: Winners advance to play each other.
items.why: Winners from round one play each other in the second round.

items.text: Conference Finals: One winner from each conference advances.
items.why: Winners of the semifinals play for the conference crown.

items.text: NBA Finals: Eastern Conference champion vs Western Conference champion.
items.why: The two conference winners play for the championship.

explanation.correct: Sixteen teams start, eight per conference. Each round is a best-of-seven, and the field halves each time: 16, 8, 4, then the two conference champions in the Finals.
explanation.incorrect: The rounds go first round, Conference Semifinals, Conference Finals, then the NBA Finals. The field halves every round until the East and West champions meet.

payload.prompt: What does 'best-of-seven' mean in the NBA playoffs?

options.text: The first team to win four games takes the series.
All seven games must be played no matter what.
Each team plays exactly seven games in a season.

explanation.correct: Best-of-seven means the series stops when one team reaches four wins. It can end 4-0, 4-1, 4-2 or 4-3, so the players only sometimes play all seven games.
explanation.incorrect: A best-of-seven does not play all seven games. It ends the moment one team has four wins, which can happen in four games.

payload.prompt: What is a sweep in the playoffs?

options.text: One team wins the series 4-0, without losing a game.
Clearing the court between games.
Winning the championship.

explanation.correct: A sweep is a 4-0 series, all four games won by one team. It is rare in the later rounds, which is why fans mention it.
explanation.incorrect: A sweep is about a single series, not the championship. It means one team won every game, 4-0.

payload.prompt: Fill in playoff series outcomes.
payload.template: In a best-of-seven series, a team must win {{wins}} games to win the series. A {{sweep}} means winning {{clean}} games in a row.

explanation.correct: The first team to four wins takes a best-of-seven. A sweep is the cleanest version of that, four wins in a row with no losses.
explanation.incorrect: A best-of-seven needs four wins to finish it, not five or seven. A sweep is four straight wins, 4-0.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: They are in the Conference Finals now.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Her team has won two playoff series and is one series from the NBA Finals.
Her team lost in the first round.
Her team has already won the championship.
Her team is playing a team from the other conference.

payload.translation: There are four rounds, and the Conference Finals is the third. Her team has won two series and now plays for its conference's spot in the NBA Finals.

followUps.why: It is a natural question that keeps her talking about her team's opponent.

followUps.line: That is one series from the Finals, right?
followUps.why: It checks your picture of the bracket in plain words, which invites her to confirm it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The Conference Finals is the third of four rounds. The winner goes to the NBA Finals against the other conference's champion.

lessons.title: The NBA Cup
lessons.objective: Explain in-season tournament groups, knockout and what counts.

payload.prompt: What is the NBA Cup (In-Season Tournament)?

options.text: A tournament held during the regular season where teams compete for a trophy and prize money, games count in the regular-season record.
The playoff championship.
A tournament only for teams below .500.

explanation.correct: Right. The NBA Cup is played during the regular season, and the wins and losses count toward each team's regular-season record.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The NBA Cup is an in-season tournament; the games count as regular-season games and teams compete for a championship and prize pool.

payload.prompt: In the Cup's group stage, do East and West teams share groups?

scene.alt: A diagram of the NBA Cup group stage: six groups of five teams, three groups of Eastern teams and three of Western teams.

choices.label: No, groups stay within a conference

explanation.correct: In the current format, each conference is split into three groups of five teams. East and West teams only meet in the Cup's final. The format has been tweaked before, so check for changes.
explanation.incorrect: Cup groups are made within each conference: three groups of five in the East and three in the West. That keeps the group games close to a normal conference schedule.

payload.prompt: After group play, how many teams advance to the NBA Cup knockout stage?

options.text: Eight: the six group winners plus a wild card from each conference.
All 30 teams continue.
Only the top two teams.

explanation.correct: Each group winner advances, and the best second-place team in each conference joins them as a wild card. That makes eight teams for the single-elimination knockout.
explanation.incorrect: Only eight teams move on: the six group winners and one wild card per conference, chosen on record. Everyone else is out of the Cup and goes back to the regular season.

payload.prompt: Match the NBA Cup structure to how it works.

pairs.definition: Teams play each other within their group, and those games count in the regular-season standings.
Single-elimination games from the quarterfinals to the final. Lose once and you are out.
A trophy and a cash prize that goes to the players on the winning team.

distractorDefinitions: A tournament held before the regular season starts.
A replacement for the All-Star Game.

explanation.summary: Group games count in the standings, and then a short knockout decides the Cup winner. The Cup is extra, not a replacement for anything.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: We won our group, so we are in the Cup knockout now.

payload.question: What is she excited about?

options.text: Her team topped its group and moves on to the Cup's single-elimination rounds.
Her team has been knocked out of the tournament.
Her team will now play only exhibition games.
Her team already won the Cup.

payload.translation: Winning the group puts her team into the knockout rounds, where one loss ends its Cup run. That is why she is excited.

followUps.why: It is a natural question, and she can tell you the matchup.
Higher-seeded Cup teams host early knockout games, so it is an informed question.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Winning the group means a place in the knockout rounds. You can just say 'Nice, who do you play first?'

lessons.title: The draft and the lottery
lessons.objective: Explain the lottery, rookie scale and tanking.

payload.prompt: What is the NBA draft lottery?

options.text: A weighted draw for the top picks: the worst teams have the best odds, but any lottery team can win.
The worst team automatically gets the first pick.
Fans vote on which player the worst team drafts.

explanation.correct: The draft lottery is a weighted drawing for the highest picks. The worst records have the best odds, but it is a real draw, so the worst team can miss out on the first pick.
explanation.incorrect: The worst team is not handed the first pick, and fans do not choose players. The lottery is weighted by record, but luck decides the top of the draft.

payload.prompt: Fill in the draft lottery rules.
payload.template: The {{num}} teams that miss the playoffs enter the lottery, and the worst team can fall no lower than the {{floor}} pick.

explanation.correct: Fourteen teams are in the lottery, and the league's rules protect the worst team from a big fall. It cannot drop below the fifth pick, though it might not get the first.
explanation.incorrect: The lottery has 14 teams, and the worst team is guaranteed one of the top five picks. It could land anywhere from first to fifth, not lower.

payload.prompt: What is tanking in basketball?

options.text: A team losing on purpose to improve its draft position.
Trading away all its stars in free agency.
Playing a slow, defense-first style.

explanation.correct: Tanking means giving up on a season, often by resting players or playing young ones, to get a better lottery position. The league flattened the lottery odds to make it less tempting.
explanation.incorrect: Tanking is about the standings, not style or trades. A team loses on purpose, usually late in a lost season, to improve its odds in the draft lottery.

payload.prompt: Match draft concepts to what they mean.

pairs.definition: Teams take college, international and other players in two rounds of 30 picks each.
A set salary scale for first-round picks, where higher picks are paid more.
A deal that lets a player split time between an NBA team and its G League affiliate.

distractorDefinitions: A contract that lasts for a single game.
A deal for a player who has retired.

explanation.summary: The draft picks the players, first-round picks get a set salary scale, and two-way deals let a young or undrafted player move between the NBA and the G League.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Their lottery odds got worse because they won too many games.

payload.question: What happened?

options.text: Her team's record improved, so its odds of a top pick dropped.
Winning games raised her team's lottery odds.
The league punished her team for winning.
Her team already clinched the playoffs.

payload.translation: Lottery odds are based on the record, and a worse record means better odds. Her team won more than expected, so its odds slid, which is a mixed blessing for a fan.

followUps.line: So winning cost you a better pick?
followUps.why: You are restating the trade-off in plain words, and she can confirm it.

followUps.line: Is it still a playoff race for you?
followUps.why: It connects the standings to the lottery, which is how fans usually think about it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The worse the record, the better the lottery odds. She may have mixed feelings about a win, and that is fine.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: They traded their first-round pick for a veteran.

payload.question: What did they do?

options.text: They sent a first-round pick to another team and got an established player back.
They drafted a veteran with that pick.
They released a veteran to free up a pick.
They bought the pick from the league.

payload.translation: The team gave away a first-round pick, usually a future one, to get a proven player right now. Teams that want to win soon often make this kind of trade.

followUps.line: So they are going for it this year?
followUps.why: It restates the idea in plain words, and she can explain what the team is chasing.
It is the natural follow-up, and it lets her tell the story.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Trading a draft pick for a veteran usually means a team is trying to win now. You can ask whether it is worth the price.

lessons.title: The salary cap in plain English
lessons.objective: Explain a soft cap, luxury tax, aprons and max contracts.

payload.prompt: Match cap concepts to how the NBA money limit works.

pairs.definition: The payroll level that governs signing free agents; about $155M in 2025-26, and reset each summer.
A cap a team can go above by using exceptions, such as re-signing its own players.
A penalty paid on payroll above the tax line, which sits well above the cap.

distractorDefinitions: A payroll limit no team is ever allowed to exceed.
A bonus paid to teams that stay under the cap.

explanation.summary: The NBA cap is soft: teams can exceed it through exceptions, and a luxury tax, starting at a higher line, is the price of going far over.

payload.prompt: What is the salary cap in the NBA?

options.text: A payroll level that limits signing free agents, but teams can exceed it through exceptions.
The highest salary any single player can make.
The total revenue the NBA makes each year.

explanation.correct: A team under the cap can sign free agents with its space, and a team over it can still re-sign its own players and use other exceptions. That is why it is called a soft cap, and the luxury tax starts higher up.
explanation.incorrect: The cap is a team payroll level, not a player's maximum or the league's revenue. It is soft, so teams can go over using exceptions, and a luxury tax applies only at a higher line.

payload.prompt: Roughly how big was the 2025-26 NBA salary cap, in millions?

explanation.correct: The 2025-26 cap was about $154.6 million per team. It is reset every summer as league revenue grows, so the newest figure is always a little higher.
explanation.incorrect: The 2025-26 NBA cap was roughly $155 million per team. It moves every summer with league revenue, so use it as a rough guide and check the current number.

payload.prompt: Match spending thresholds to their names and effects.

pairs.definition: A spending line above the tax. Over it, a team loses some ways to add salary in trades and signings.
A higher line with stricter limits and heavier penalties, including on future draft picks.
The most a player can be paid, set as a share of the cap that rises with years of service.

distractorDefinitions: A discount for players who go undrafted.
A bonus for winning the playoffs.

explanation.summary: The aprons sit above the tax line and make it harder for a big spender to add salary. A max contract is the most any one player can earn, based on the cap.

payload.prompt: What happens when a team goes over the luxury tax line?

options.text: It pays a tax to the league on the amount over, at a higher rate if it keeps doing it.
It is removed from the league's standings.
It must trade its best player.

explanation.correct: A team over the tax line pays a tax on every dollar above it, and teams that keep going over pay a steeper repeater rate. That is why owners often dump salary before the line.
explanation.incorrect: The tax is a money penalty, not a removal from the league or a forced trade. The team pays on each dollar over the line, and repeat offenders pay more.

payload.prompt: About how high was the 2025-26 luxury tax line, in millions?

explanation.correct: The 2025-26 tax line was about $187.9 million, roughly $33 million above the cap. It is reset each summer, so treat the number as an example of the gap, not a constant.
explanation.incorrect: The 2025-26 tax line was roughly $188 million per team, well above the cap of about $155 million. Both numbers move each summer, but the tax line always sits above the cap.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: They are right at the first apron, so they may have to shed salary.

payload.question: What is she describing?

options.text: The team's payroll is at a line where extra spending brings tighter limits.
The team has cap space and should sign someone.
The team is under the salary cap and can do anything.
The team has already traded its best player.

payload.translation: The first apron is a payroll line above the luxury tax. Past it, a team gets fewer tools for adding salary, so she thinks the team may need to trim payroll to stay flexible.

followUps.line: Are they trying to get under it?
followUps.why: It asks whether the team plans to cut salary, which is the usual response.
It lets her talk about the roster without you needing the contract details.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The apron is a payroll line. You do not need the exact number: 'are they trying to get under it?' is a solid question.

lessons.title: Trades, free agency and contract types
lessons.objective: Decode player options, sign-and-trades and buyouts.

payload.prompt: Match the offseason moves to how they work.

pairs.definition: Teams swap players or picks. Both teams must agree, and the league checks it fits the cap rules.
Players whose contracts expired can sign with other teams, starting in late June or early July.
A player re-signs with his team, which then trades him to the team he wants to join.

distractorDefinitions: A player is released and must sit out a year.
A coach decides which players to keep.

explanation.summary: Trades swap players between teams, free agency is open to players with expired contracts, and a sign-and-trade combines the two to let a departing player move teams.

payload.prompt: What is a restricted free agent?

options.text: A player whose old team can match any offer he gets from another team.
A player who is injured and cannot play.
A player banned for breaking league rules.

explanation.correct: A restricted free agent can sign offer sheets with other teams, but his current team has the right to match and keep him. That makes outside teams wary of making an offer.
explanation.incorrect: It has nothing to do with injuries or bans. Restricted means the player's old team can match any offer from another team, so he is not fully free to leave.

payload.prompt: Match contract options to who controls them.

pairs.definition: The player decides whether to play the next season on his contract or become a free agent.
The team decides whether to keep the player for the next season or let the contract end.
A player agrees to take less than the money left on his deal so he can leave the team.

distractorDefinitions: A contract that can never be changed.
An option that only rookies are allowed to have.

explanation.summary: The player controls a player option, the team controls a team option, and a buyout is a negotiated exit where the player gives up some pay.

payload.prompt: What is a trade exception in the salary cap rules?

options.text: Room a team earns by trading away more salary than it takes back, to absorb a player later.
Permission to trade without league approval.
A player who does not count against the cap.

explanation.correct: When a team trades away more salary than it gets back, it gets a trade exception for the difference. It can take on a player up to that amount later, even over the cap, but only for a limited time.
explanation.incorrect: A trade exception is not a player or an approval waiver. It is a credit from an earlier trade that lets a team absorb salary in a later one.

payload.prompt: A star says he is leaving in free agency. Trade him now?

situation.narrative: Your team's star is on an expiring contract and his agent has said he plans to test free agency. The team is not a contender, and several teams want to trade for him.

options.label: Trade him now for picks and young players
options.consequence: The team gets assets in return instead of losing him for nothing in the summer. The risk is that he would have stayed after all, which his agent has said is unlikely.
considerations: A trade brings picks or young players
He has said he plans to leave
The team is not contending this season anyway

options.label: Offer him the biggest contract allowed
options.consequence: It costs nothing to ask, and he might say yes. If he has already decided to leave, the team loses its best trade window.
considerations: It can be a real last attempt to keep him
He has already signaled he wants out
If he refuses, trade interest may fade

options.label: Wait until free agency and see what happens
options.consequence: If he leaves, the team gets nothing back. It gave up its leverage and the market.
considerations: No return if he signs elsewhere
Trade offers are best before the deadline
It only works if he would re-sign anyway

payload.expertNote: When a star has signaled he will leave and the team is not a contender, front offices usually trade him for assets. A contender, or a star who wants to stay, is a different conversation.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: They have a big trade exception they can use this summer.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The team has salary-cap flexibility from a previous trade and can absorb a big contract from another team.
The team can trade anyone without approval.
The team is allowed one trade per year.
The team can trade for a player who is injured.

payload.translation: She means the team earned trade exception flexibility in an earlier trade and can use it to acquire a player from another team, absorbing salary that would normally put them over the cap.

followUps.line: Perfect chance to get a star.
followUps.why: Recognizing that trade exceptions give teams flexibility to make mid-market acquisitions.

followUps.line: How long does the exception last?
followUps.why: A good follow-up; trade exceptions expire, so timing matters.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Trade exceptions are cap flexibility earned from past trades. Use them to absorb salary without exceeding your cap.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: They bought him out instead of trading him.

payload.question: What happened?

options.text: The team paid part of the player's remaining contract to release him and end their relationship.
The team sold their ownership stake.
The team purchased the player's house.
The team signed a new player.

payload.translation: She means the team and player agreed to mutually end the contract early. The team paid part of what he was owed so he could leave and sign elsewhere.

followUps.line: So he is free to sign anywhere now.
followUps.why: Recognizing that a bought-out player becomes a free agent.

followUps.line: That costs them money to lose him.
followUps.why: A good follow-up understanding that buyouts are expensive for teams.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A buyout is when a team pays a player to leave. It costs money but gives both sides a clean break.

lessons.title: The calendar: deadline to summer
lessons.objective: Place the trade deadline, draft, free agency and summer league on the year.

payload.prompt: Order the offseason events from spring through summer.

items.text: Trade deadline in February: last day teams can make mid-season trades.
items.why: Happens during the regular season, last chance to add or subtract before playoffs.

items.text: NBA draft lottery in May: lottery teams find out draft order.
items.why: Held after regular season ends; determines which team gets which pick.

items.text: NBA draft in June: teams select college and international players.
items.why: Happens right before free agency; new rookies and draft picks are announced.

items.text: Free agency begins in June: unrestricted players can sign with new teams.
items.why: Starts right after draft; free agents negotiate with new teams.

items.text: Summer League in July: rookies and young players play exhibition games.
items.why: Happens last; develops young talent and evaluates draft picks and roster moves.

explanation.correct: Perfect. That is the exact offseason calendar from trade deadline through summer league.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The offseason order is: trade deadline, lottery, draft, free agency, then summer league.

payload.prompt: Order the urgency of trades relative to the deadline.

items.text: Early season trades: teams explore moves to add star power or depth.
items.why: Happens when the team is still evaluating; less urgent.

items.text: Mid-season moves: contenders add players to boost playoff odds.
items.why: Happens as teams solidify their playoff position; moderate urgency.

items.text: Deadline day trades: frantic last-minute moves by contenders and sellers.
items.why: Last day to trade; highest urgency as buyers and sellers make final deals.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Trade deadline urgency builds as February arrives and teams make final pushes.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Trades happen all season, but urgency peaks near the February deadline as contenders and sellers make their moves.

payload.prompt: When is the NBA trade deadline?

options.text: Mid-February; the last day teams can make trades before the playoffs start.
June 15, before free agency.
October 1, before the season starts.

explanation.correct: Right. The trade deadline is typically mid-February, giving contenders a last chance to add pieces.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The trade deadline is in mid-February, during the regular season. It is the last day teams can trade.

payload.prompt: What is NBA Summer League?

options.text: Exhibition games in July featuring draft picks, young players and free agents to develop talent and evaluate rosters.
The official championship tournament.
Weekend games for fans only.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Summer League is where rookies and young players debut, develop skills and compete for roster spots.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Summer League is an exhibition series in July where draft picks and young players play in a real-game environment.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: The trade deadline is coming up and they might make a move.

payload.question: What is she anticipating?

options.text: The team is approaching mid-February and might trade for another player to improve the team's chances.
The season is ending.
The draft happens tomorrow.
Free agency just opened.

payload.translation: She means the team is nearing the February trade deadline and might add or subtract players to position themselves for a playoff push or rebuild.

followUps.why: Recognizing a specific need the team might address by trading.

followUps.line: Or they might sell if they are out of it.
followUps.why: A good follow-up understanding that contenders buy and non-contenders sell at the deadline.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The trade deadline in February is when contenders add and rebuilding teams sell. It is the last chance to trade mid-season.
